In 1970, outside a New York apartment she and her husband were considering, 24-year-old Jaclyn Smith found herself talking with Warren Beatty about a possible film role. 

Her first husband, actor Roger Davis, was upstairs with their realtor. She would only learn the full truth later.
They had met at a commercial casting call in 1968 and married within months. 

Smith later described how well-matched they seemed at the time: neither drank, both loved architecture, both were Southern actors, and they liked the same food. 

She was young, romantic, and still believed marriage meant permanence. Then Beatty appeared and offered her an audition. 

Before she could answer, Davis materialized and shut it down, telling Beatty that his wife only did commercials. What Smith later discovered made the moment cruel: while she stood on the sidewalk, Davis had been upstairs with the realtor. 

The realtor’s husband eventually exposed the affair; the realtor confirmed it. Davis denied and deflected. Smith reached her limit after finding him with another woman on their fourth wedding anniversary. 

They divorced in 1975.

She tried again with actor Dennis Cole. They met through Charlie’s Angels, dated for about a year and a half, and married in a deliberately secret New York ceremony in 1978 with only 25 guests, phone invitations, and decoy hotel reservations. 

By then Smith was no longer the same wide-eyed bride. She discovered Cole’s infidelity through a note in his pocket; career tension added to the strain. The marriage ended in 1981.

What came next was different. While filming Nightkill (1980), she met British cinematographer Anthony B. Richmond. 

He proposed after only a month or two. Their small wedding included three friends and three dogs. They married in 1981. Their son Gaston was born in 1982; daughter Spencer-Margaret followed in 1985. 

Smith has spoken of those years with genuine affection and credited Richmond as a devoted partner, but alcohol and drugs eroded the marriage. 

She could not live inside the chaos addiction brought with it. They divorced in 1989. Years later she spoke of his eventual sobriety with respect rather than bitterness.

In 1991, while her father was undergoing heart surgery, Smith met surgeon Brad Allen, who was part of the medical team. They dated for years—including a long stretch of long-distance living while he worked in Chicago and she raised her children in Los Angeles. 

After three marriages, two children, betrayal, and addiction, she was still willing to believe that marriage itself had not been the mistake. 

When they married in Los Angeles in 1997, her children were part of the day: 11-year-old Spencer-Margaret served as maid of honor and 15-year-old Gaston gave his mother away. 

Nearly three decades later, Allen remains the man she points to when she talks about finally getting it right. She has said he is the best stepfather she could have hoped for and that he truly loves her children. 

She kept believing long enough to find the family she wanted. 🌹

Elon Musk took a $40,000 username from a guy who had owned it for 16 years.

He paid him absolutely nothing.
Not even a dollar.

Instead, he was offered a T-shirt and a tour of Twitter’s headquarters.

This is the story of Gene X. Hwang the first @X username 

2007

- photographer from San Francisco
- co-founder of Orange Photography
- registers @x on Twitter
- keeps the username for 16 years

over the years

account grows to ~53,000 followers
receives offers of up to $40,000 for the handle

But he refuses to sell

2014

- hackers steal his x account
- Twitter helps him recover it

July 23, 2023

- Elon Musk announces Twitter will become X
- Gene is in Canada playing in a pinball tournament

He has no idea what’s coming

July 25, 2023

- Twitter officially becomes X
- the company wants x
- Gene receives an email from Twitter support

“Your user handle is affiliated with X Corp.”

his username is taken and gets a new one @x12345678998765

what X offers him

- company merchandise
- exclusive tour of X headquarters
- meeting with the management team

$0.

Gene even asks if he can have the old blue Twitter bird sign being removed from headquarters.

they say no.

October 2025

X launches its Handle Marketplace
rare usernames can cost $2,500 to over $1 MILLION

users must maintain a paid subscription
lose the subscription, potentially lose the handle

the same company that took x without paying its owner now charges people for access to rare usernames.

16 years building an identity.

$40,000 in offers rejected.

and all he got was an offer of merchandise and an office tour.

BROTHER.

Adam Robinson died Sunday in a jet crash with his wife and two little kids.

He built tools that take an anonymous visit to a website and turn it into a real name and contact info. His company kept a digital file on people.

That's the raw material of a surveillance state. Data like this doesn't stay in marketing. It gets bought, merged, and fed into the same systems that track where you go, what you read, and who you are.

But he did it differently. He bootstrapped everything. He never took big VC money, and there was no board pushing him to grow the data as fast as possible or sell to someone bigger. He kept his companies lean and profitable, so he got to decide how far the data went, who got it, and under what rules.

Most founders in this space lose that option once the money comes in.

A surveillance state runs on cheap, easy access to personal information. It doesn't love founders who can say no and stay independent.

Who controls these companies matters more than people realize. When the founder still has control, the limits stay tight. When he doesn't, the data flows wherever the power wants it.

In May 2025, I painted a mural of Donald Trump titled The Host. The mural was an image if Donald Trump, dressed as Uncle Sam with the Israeli flag in his eyes.

The work was a commentary on how US politics and foreign policy have been co-opted by Israel.

Shortly after its completion, police were called to the mural, a campaign was launched to pressure @innerwestcouncil into removing it (which they did), and I began receiving legal letters.

What followed was a lengthy legal process in which the complainant sought orders from the Tribunal requiring me to:

1. I create a new mural that apologised for the original mural, and that this mural had to be in the same place as the old mural;
2. I had to post photos of the mural apology and post it on my Instagram page;
3. I had to write a letter of apology to the President of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, and prescribed what he wanted me to write in that letter;
4. I pay $10,000 + revenue made on the sale of posters of the mural in equal parts to several Jewish fundraisers; and
5. I was to attend the Sydney Jewish Museum and undertake specific case studies.

After more than a year, I’ve finally put that legal process behind me.

This is yet another in a growing list of attempts to silence and censor my artwork critical of Israel. 

Long story short, it didn’t work. 👊

I owe an enormous debt of gratitude to Jen Robinson, Danielle, Michael and Lauren at Marque Lawyers, and Oshie Fagir.

You are absolute lifesavers ❤️🙏💪
